item.title: Data Centers Are Funding the Energy Technology All Buildings Will Benefit From
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
Battery storage is getting cheaper

The post Data Centers Are Funding the Energy Technology All Buildings Will Benefit From appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
3 min agoOct. 28, 2026 4:02 pm

The energy technology that commercial buildings have been circling for years, on-site storage, microgrid controls, islanding capability, is getting cheaper and more capable at a pace nobody in real estate paid for. Data centers are driving it. Facing grid constraints severe enough to stall multi-billion dollar projects, the AI buildout has poured capital into solving energy problems that building owners share but could never have funded on their own. The solutions are portable, and they are arriving in the commercial market as a byproduct.

US data center electricity demand climbed from roughly 23 gigawatts in 2023 to about 42 in 2026, and the forecasts for where it goes next are large enough that the range between them exceeds what most sectors consume in total. Deloitte projects 176 gigawatts by 2035. Goldman Sachs expects US data center power demand to more than double between 2025 and 2027. McKinsey attributes roughly three quarters of all US power demand growth through 2030 to the sector.

The grid was not built for that, and it cannot be rebuilt quickly. Around 2 terawatts of generation and storage capacity sits in US interconnection queues, close to twice the currently installed fleet, with a median wait from request to commercial operation now exceeding five years. Northern Virginia connections can take more than seven years. Texas has 86 gigawatts of pending interconnection requests through 2031, roughly equal to the state’s entire existing grid capacity.

Faced with waits that long, data center developers stopped treating grid power as the only option. On-site generation, large-scale battery deployments, and behind-the-meter microgrids moved from contingency planning into primary strategy, backed by capital at a scale the energy technology sector had never seen from a single customer segment. The industry had to become an energy player because the alternative was not building.

Commercial energy storage has needed volume to bring costs down for a decade, and data centers are supplying it. The microgrid battery storage market is projected to grow from $8.4 billion in 2026 to $39 billion by 2035, with manufacturing capacity and cost curves responding to demand that originates almost entirely outside commercial real estate. A property owner evaluating storage in 2027 will price hardware that got cheaper because hyperscalers needed it first.

The same dynamic is working through the controls layer. Managing a facility that generates its own power, stores it, and decides moment to moment whether to draw from the grid requires software that did not exist in mature form a few years ago. Data center operators funded that development because their uptime requirements left no room for it to work poorly. Islanding capability, the ability to disconnect from utility lines and run independently while keeping local loads served, now ships in commercial hybrid inverters as a standard feature rather than a custom engineering project.

Utilities are adapting in ways that extend the benefit further. Several have introduced expedited permitting and interconnection pathways for projects that can demonstrate flexible load or on-site generation, since a customer able to reduce consumption during peak events is easier to serve than one who cannot. Incentive programs for demand response and behind-the-meter storage have expanded in the markets where capacity is tightest, reflecting a calculation that paying existing customers to shift load costs less than building new transmission.

For commercial buildings, energy investments are an easier sell. Demand charges, which bill based on a customer’s highest consumption, get more expensive as grid capacity tightens. On-site storage addresses that directly. The same equipment qualifies for utility incentive payments and can earn revenue through demand response participation.

Buildings able to island are also worth more to the grid than they used to be. A property that can separate itself during a stress event removes demand from a constrained system at the moment that demand is most expensive to serve. Aggregated across enough sites, that capability starts to function as dispatchable capacity, and virtual power plant programs are beginning to treat commercial buildings accordingly. Commercial real estate has been described as the largest untapped distributed energy resource available to address US grid shortages, and the technology to access it is arriving on someone else’s development budget.

Constraints remain. Battery supply chains are tight, transformers are quoted in years rather than months, and several states have begun imposing review requirements on large loads that may slow the data center buildout driving all of this. Texas passed SB 6 last year, adding a six-month review for projects above 75 megawatts along with new interconnection costs and curtailment requirements.

We are likely to see the gap between what a sophisticated data center can do with energy and what a well-run commercial building can do continue to narrow. The same cutting-edge techniques being developed at data centers will eventually become commonplace. Love or hate data centers they have to get credit for pushing utilities and industry to move faster when it comes to adopting much needed energy technology.

item.title: CoStar Pushes Into Aerial Imaging With $730M Vexcel Buy
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
CoStar Group will pay $730 million for aerial imaging firm Vexcel, combining sky and ground photography to expand its AI-driven property database.

The post CoStar Pushes Into Aerial Imaging With $730M Vexcel Buy appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
CoStar Group agreed to acquire Vexcel, an aerial imaging company, for $730 million in cash. Vexcel uses manned aircraft and proprietary technology to capture high-resolution aerial photographs across 45 countries, generating $140 million in revenue over the last 12 months, up 30% year-over-year. CoStar plans to integrate Vexcel’s aerial photography with its ground-level property database and apply artificial intelligence to extract data from the images. Erik Jorgensen will remain CEO of Vexcel, which will continue operating under its own brand.

CoStar has relied on vehicle-mounted cameras to photograph buildings for its property database. The company sees Vexcel’s aerial platform as a complement to that ground-based approach, enabling broader property coverage and new data extraction capabilities through AI. CoStar CEO Andy Florance said the company’s 2,000-person sales team can accelerate Vexcel’s growth beyond its current six-person sales force. The deal follows CoStar’s $1.6 billion acquisition of 3D imaging firm Matterport, which closed in February, and its $815 million purchase of housing data provider Zonda in August.

CoStar reported third-quarter revenue of $952 million, up 14% year-over-year, and raised its full-year guidance. But shares fell more than 13% after the earnings release, extending a 65% decline over the past year. Investors focused on annualized net new bookings, which dropped to $37 million from $84 million a year earlier. Florance attributed the decline to economic headwinds and slower sales force growth, prompting analysts at BTIG and Jefferies to lower their price targets for the stock.

item.title: How Real Estate Organizations Can Avoid the AI Adoption J-Curve
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Studio
item.description:
Learn how commercial real estate firms can manage the AI deployment J-curve, accelerate adoption, prove value, and build effective governance.

The post How Real Estate Organizations Can Avoid the AI Adoption J-Curve appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
The J-curve is a familiar concept in private equity and economics. Performance declines before it improves, and the shape of that trajectory looks like the letter J. Anyone who has managed a significant technology deployment has experienced a version of it firsthand. New systems disrupt established workflows. People who were productive on the old process become temporarily less productive on the new one. Support tickets spike, workarounds proliferate, and for a period of weeks or months the organization is measurably worse off than it was before the investment. AI deployments in commercial real estate are producing exactly this pattern, and the depth and duration of that dip is where most of the difference between successful and failed initiatives actually lives.

The first and most consequential decision that determines the shape of that curve is made before any technology is deployed. It is the expectation that gets set with leadership about what the initiative will accomplish and when. “A typical mistake we see is treating the early productivity dip as evidence that AI isn’t working.” said Chris Campbell, Managing Director of Technology Advisory at JLL. “The J-curve is a normal part of transformation. The objective isn’t to eliminate the dip, but to manage it deliberately and shorten the time it takes to get to measurable results.” That fear is understandable. A team requesting budget for an AI initiative is competing against other priorities, and the temptation to promise transformative results in the first quarter is real. But an initiative that promises too much creates a much steeper J-curve, because the gap between what was promised and what materializes in the early months reads as failure rather than as the expected transition period. 

AI has the ability to transform even the hardest tasks needed by a real estate organization. But it can’t do so right away. Realistic expectations are what makes the transition from pilot to production possible. A pilot that was promised to deliver a 40% productivity improvement and delivers 12% gets shut down. A pilot that was promised to deliver 10% and delivers 12% gets expanded. The technology performed identically in both cases. What differed was the framing, and the framing determines whether leadership sees a promising foundation or a failed experiment. Getting that framing right at the outset is the cheapest and most effective way to protect an AI program through its most vulnerable phase.

The people involved in an AI deployment are the other variable that determines how quickly an organization climbs out of the dip. The employees who will be building these systems and the ones whose daily work will change as a result are the ones who can either accelerate adoption or quietly resist it. Keeping them engaged through the transition requires visible progress, which means starting with projects small enough to produce results quickly. “Productivity can be difficult to measure at an enterprise level, particularly in an AI program. We encourage clients to start by identifying specific, repeatable work that can be done faster, better or differently, and then measure the outcome,” Campbell said. A general claim that AI has improved efficiency across an organization is easy to dismiss. A concrete example of a specific team that stopped spending six hours a week on a particular task is not. “You can start small in order to get these really good examples of how it is making people’s jobs better, not just more efficient,” Campbell said. That distinction matters more than it might appear. Efficiency is an organizational benefit. A better job is a personal one, and personal benefits are what drive the enthusiasm that carries an initiative through its difficult phase.

Identifying champions early, and doing so across functions rather than concentrating them in a technology group, is one of the strongest predictors of whether an AI program scales successfully. “We have seen good success with clients that have embedded champions in multiple different functions,” Campbell said. “Champions need to understand the current workflow at a granular level, including the workarounds and friction points that rarely show up in a process map, in order to redesign work, rather than simply automating it.” That granular business knowledge is what separates a useful champion from a well-intentioned one. Understanding how work actually gets done, including the informal steps and workarounds that never appear in a process document, is what allows a champion to identify where AI will genuinely help and where it will create friction. Someone who understands the technology but not the workflow will consistently propose solutions to problems that do not exist.

Those champions typically get formalized into a committee with its own governance structure and mandate, and the effectiveness of that committee depends heavily on whether it has clear priorities to work against. Strategic alignment to business goals is the starting point, but the specific criteria that guide decisions matter just as much. Resilience, cost optimization, and user experience are all legitimate priorities, and they sometimes conflict. A committee that has explicitly ranked them can make consistent decisions about which projects to pursue and which to defer. A committee that has not, tends to relitigate the same tradeoffs with every proposal.

One responsibility that these committees increasingly own is the lifecycle management of AI agents, which is a genuinely new organizational function that most companies have not built infrastructure for. Agents get deployed for specific purposes, and those purposes change or disappear over time. Without a clear process for retiring them, organizations accumulate agents that run without oversight, consume budget, and occasionally produce outputs that nobody is reviewing. “An AI agent performing a business task needs many of the same disciplines we apply to people: a defined role, appropriate training, clear boundaries, performance management, and ultimately a decision about whether it should continue doing the work,” Campbell said. That framing is useful because it brings a familiar management discipline to an unfamiliar problem. Organizations already know how to onboard, train, evaluate, and offboard employees. Applying that same structure to AI agents gives the committee a workable model for governance rather than requiring them to invent one.

The J-curve in AI deployment is not entirely avoidable. Any meaningful change to how work gets done will produce a period of adjustment, and organizations that expect to skip that phase are setting themselves up for the exact disappointment they are trying to avoid. What is controllable is the depth of the dip and the speed of the recovery. Realistic expectations set with leadership from the start, small early projects that produce concrete and personally meaningful wins, champions embedded across functions who understand the business at a granular level, and governance structures that treat AI agents with the same rigor applied to any other organizational resource all shorten that curve considerably. The organizations that build those foundations are not the ones that avoid the difficult phase of AI adoption. They are the ones that get through it fast enough to still have leadership support on the other side.

item.title: Tech Has Turned Parking From a Cost Center to a Revenue Driver
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
AI-powered parking management helps commercial properties reduce revenue leakage, optimize pricing, boost NOI, and improve customer experience.

The post Tech Has Turned Parking From a Cost Center to a Revenue Driver appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Most commercial properties have a parking operation, and most property management teams have nobody responsible for running it. Leasing has a team. Maintenance has a team. Parking has a vendor contract, a rate sheet that was set some years ago, and whoever happens to notice when something breaks.

That arrangement produces predictable results. Revenue leakage, the gap between what should be collected and what actually is, runs 10 to 25 percent at properties without active monitoring. Underpricing costs the average multifamily property around $100,000 a year in missed net operating income. Neither number shows up as a problem on a report because nobody is generating the report.

The labor requirement that once made dedicated parking management expensive has largely been automated away. License plate recognition handles enforcement, mobile payment handles collection, and gateless entry removes the equipment that used to need someone standing near it. That does not mean staffing disappears everywhere. Shareena Sandbrook, Chief Commercial Development Officer at Towne, is careful to distinguish between the properties where automation is the whole answer and the ones where it is not. “The tech has come a long way to help reduce the labor but for some types of parking, particularly healthcare, humans are still a really important touch point,” she said. Someone arriving at a hospital is having a difficult day, and a kiosk is not the right greeting.

Where the technology has moved recently is from executing tasks to finding money. Automation made parking cheaper to run. AI is making it more productive, and Sandbrook describes the shift as the system doing analysis nobody at the property had the capacity to do. “AI not only makes our tech faster, it can now identify opportunities to increase NOI by predicting utilization, pricing suggestions, and competitive analysis,” she said. “There is always some revenue leakage not identified, particularly if there isn’t someone specifically working on managing it.”

Speed is its own revenue lever in some asset classes. A retail center where it takes eight minutes to find a space and exit the garage has converted shopping time into waiting time, and the tenant whose sales suffer is the one paying rent. Reducing friction at entry and exit does not show up on a parking P&L, but it shows up in the center’s performance.

Dynamic pricing has gone from unfamiliar to expected over a relatively short period. Rates that move with demand, time of day, or local conditions once required explaining to every customer who encountered them. “When we first started no one really understood surge pricing, now they are much more used to the idea,” Sandbrook said. Consumer familiarity with variable pricing in ridesharing and travel did most of that work before parking operators had to.

What AI adds is the ability to price against information the property does not generate itself. Local event schedules, competitor rates, weather forecasts, and seasonal patterns all affect what a space is worth on a given afternoon, and a pricing engine that reads those signals can adjust faster than a manager reviewing rates quarterly. The target in most cases is somewhere around 85 to 90 percent utilization, high enough to capture demand without turning away the marginal customer.

Older properties face a real obstacle in getting there, since the equipment and software carry upfront cost against a revenue stream the owner has never counted on. Sandbrook sees third-party arrangements as the way most of those properties end up making the investment, because they let an owner see results before committing capital. “One of the benefits of working with third parties is that they can start to realize the benefits without putting up too much money,” she said. “Once they start to realize what kinds of revenue can be made they usually are ready for more investment.”

The sums involved tend to surprise owners who have treated parking as infrastructure. “The additional revenue could be in the hundreds of thousands of dollars in revenue which, depending on the cap rates could really improve the property’s value,” Sandbrook said. Parking income is typically capitalized somewhere between 5 and 10 percent, so a few hundred thousand dollars of durable annual NOI can move a valuation by millions. That math is available at properties that already have the garage built and the cars already arriving.

Parking is also the first and last thing most people experience at a building, which makes it an operational question regardless of what it earns. The properties doing well on both counts have generally stopped treating it as something to be contracted out and forgotten.

item.title: UPS Targets Data Center Logistics as New Revenue Driver
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
UPS sees a $15 billion logistics opportunity in data center growth as it targets high-margin shipments to replace lost Amazon volume.

The post UPS Targets Data Center Logistics as New Revenue Driver appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
UPS told investors it sees a $15 billion logistics opportunity tied to data center growth, a market the company is targeting to offset volume losses from its ended partnership with Amazon. CEO Carol Tomé highlighted the opportunity during an Oct. 27 earnings call, as UPS reported a 4.2% decline in package volumes but a 7% increase in average revenue per package. Revenue growth came from healthcare shipments and the company’s returns business, Happy Returns.

Data center logistics are growing faster than traditional package delivery, according to Matt Guffey, UPS’s chief U.S. domestic officer. He said the company is positioned to handle the complex supply chain requirements of data centers, an area where UPS has been investing in cold chain and other specialized capabilities to differentiate from competitors. The shipping company also identified automotive and tech sectors as growth areas.

UPS has been shedding low-margin Amazon volume since the two agreed to wind down their partnership last year. Amazon had negotiated significant shipping discounts due to its scale, compressing UPS’s per-package revenue. The Atlanta-based company delivered 46 million fewer packages in the second quarter of 2026 compared to the prior year as that partnership concluded.

Amazon announced in May it would enter supply chain logistics for large companies, but UPS leadership said it has not seen meaningful business impact. CEO Tomé told investors the two companies operate different networks. Industry observers note Amazon has capital to invest in specialized logistics if it chooses, though it currently serves a different customer base than UPS and FedEx.

item.title: Rental Fee Rules Are Moving to Cities and States, Creating a Compliance Headache
item.dc:creator: Franco Faraudo
item.description:
States and cities are tightening rental fee laws, requiring transparent pricing, limiting landlord charges, and raising compliance risks for operators.

The post Rental Fee Rules Are Moving to Cities and States, Creating a Compliance Headache appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Federal attention to rental fee practices has receded over the past year, and the vacuum has not gone unfilled. State legislatures and city councils have taken up the issue on their own, producing a growing set of rules that govern what landlords can charge, how those charges have to be disclosed, and what happens when they get it wrong.

Seattle passed the most recent example in August. The city council voted 8-0 to approve the Rental Fee Restriction Ordinance, which takes effect July 1, 2027. The law bans recurring pet rent along with charges for package and mail handling, common area access, valet garbage, in-unit appliances, lease administration, and adding or removing a tenant from a lease. Landlords can still collect application screening fees, utilities, key replacement charges, security deposits, and pet deposits capped at 25 percent of rent. Move-in fees are limited to one month’s rent in total.

The disclosure requirements may matter more than the prohibitions. Seattle will require advertisements, listings, applications, and leases to present base rent, all mandatory and optional fees, and utility estimates on a standardized summary sheet. The Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections gets enforcement authority and subpoena power, and the City Attorney’s Office can recover three times the amount of any illegal fees collected.

Colorado moved earlier and went further in some respects. House Bill 25-1090 took effect January 1, 2026, and requires landlords to advertise a single total price that incorporates every mandatory charge. The law bans common area maintenance fees outright and caps third-party markups at either 2 percent of the landlord’s actual cost or $10 a month, whichever is lower. For leases of a year or less, non-utility fees cannot increase more than 2 percent during the term. Tenants who paid a prohibited fee can send a written demand for reimbursement.

Connecticut took a disclosure-focused approach with Public Act 25-44, signed in June 2025 with rental provisions effective that October. Landlords must include all periodic or recurring fees in any advertised rent, whether or not a tenant can opt out of them. Payment processing fees, pet fees and deposits, utilities, and damage charges are excepted. A violation entitles the tenant to one month’s rent plus attorney’s fees.

Tracking this as it develops is becoming part of the job for anyone running a portfolio across multiple jurisdictions, and Krisann Gaiko, SVP of Learning and Enablement at Grace Hill, argues that waiting for passage is too late. Knowing what is under consideration gives operators time to adjust before a deadline and a chance to participate in the process. “Managers and VPs need to know what laws are being proposed so they can be prepared operationally and advocate politically,” she said.

The practical difficulty is that the people closest to these properties have no capacity to do that monitoring themselves. “Property operators are drowning in the day to day, it is a lot to ask them to read every new law or legislation,” Gaiko said. A regional manager handling leasing, maintenance escalations, and staffing across a dozen communities is not going to read a city council agenda, which puts the burden on corporate compliance functions that are often thin.

Writing a compliant policy is also only the first half of the work. Gaiko describes the second half as translating that policy into procedures the people executing them can actually follow, which requires asking those people what would have to change. “You have to sit down and put policies together that are compliant,” she said. “From there, you have to bring your teams in and ask them how the procedures need to change to match that policy.” A fee disclosure requirement touches leasing scripts, listing templates, application flows, lease documents, and onboarding materials, and none of that updates itself.

Compliance that was verified at rollout and never checked again tends to drift as staff turns over and shortcuts accumulate, which is how an operator ends up out of compliance without anyone having decided to be. Creating protocols around compliance only works if the procedures being run by staff continue to adhere to the protocols, requiring ongoing audits.

Gaiko also thinks the industry has a self-inflicted problem underneath the regulatory one. Fees that serve a real purpose get resented when nobody explains what they cover, and fees that cannot be explained probably should not be charged. “People perceive these as junk fees because landlords are not explaining them well,” she said. “If you can’t defend the fees then it probably should not exist.”

Where this ends up, in her view, is somewhere operators may find they prefer. All-in pricing removes the gap between the advertised number and the actual monthly cost, which removes the moment where a prospect feels misled. “All-in rent pricing can turn out to be a good experience,” Gaiko said. “It creates trust and can make for a better relationship.”

Several of these laws have compliance dates that have not yet arrived, and more jurisdictions are drafting their own versions. Operators working across state lines will be managing different disclosure formats, different prohibited fee lists, and different penalty structures in each market, with the Seattle rules landing in mid-2027 and Colorado’s already in force.

The post Rental Fee Rules Are Moving to Cities and States, Creating a Compliance Headache appeared first on Propmodo.

item.title: Long Island City Rental Tower Hits 90% Leased Before Opening
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
The Orchard in Long Island City reached 90% leased 10 months into marketing and a year before its 2027 opening.

The post Long Island City Rental Tower Hits 90% Leased Before Opening appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
The Orchard, a 70-story rental tower in Long Island City, reached 90% leased after 10 months of marketing and more than a year before its early 2027 opening. Construction wrapped last year on the 824-unit project, developed by BLDG Management Co. under CEO Lloyd Goldman. The building also signed its first retail tenants — K-beauty brand Tokimo, Japanese tea and beverage brand Mollytea, and financial tech firm Intuit — filling nearly all of its 7,500 square feet of ground-floor space. Corcoran New Developments serves as exclusive leasing agent.

At 823 feet, the tower claims the title of tallest building in Queens, surpassing the nearby Skyline Tower’s 778 feet. It ranks as the second-tallest building in New York outside Manhattan, behind only Brooklyn Tower. The project includes more than 100,000 square feet of amenities, anchored by a 60,000-square-foot landscaped recreation area that the developer calls the city’s largest private backyard. Of the 824 apartments, 576 are market-rate and 248 affordable.

Preleasing performance at The Orchard reflects continued demand for new rental inventory in Long Island City, which has emerged as one of the city’s most active residential development districts. The tower sits near the foot of the 59th Street Bridge in a neighborhood that has added thousands of units over the past decade. Strong absorption ahead of delivery suggests renters remain willing to commit to properties offering large amenity packages and location advantages, even as the broader New York rental market contends with elevated supply.

The Orchard — Queens’ Tallest Building — Is Almost All Leased Out Ahead of 2027 Opening

item.content:encoded:
As office markets continue to adjust to shifting tenant demand, evolving workplace expectations, and changing investment conditions, owners and operators face new challenges in positioning their portfolios for long-term performance. Tenants are rethinking not just how much space they need but how they use it, and buildings that can adapt to those changing needs are better positioned to attract and keep occupiers. This webinar explores the trends shaping the office market heading into 2027 and the strategies investors and asset managers are using to navigate uncertainty, optimize portfolios, and identify opportunities. From evaluating asset performance and repositioning properties to adapting leasing strategies and creating flexible workspaces that evolve with tenants, discover how industry leaders are approaching the next phase of the office market.

item.title: Office-to-Residential Pipeline Restarts After Summer Structural Scare
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
New York's office conversion pipeline restarts after July structural failure, with 16 new permits issued and heightened scrutiny from lenders and developers.

The post Office-to-Residential Pipeline Restarts After Summer Structural Scare appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
New York’s office-to-apartment conversion activity has resumed after a July structural failure at the former Pfizer headquarters building halted projects and triggered citywide inspections. Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said the city has issued initial construction permits for 16 new projects since the accident, which caused two structural columns to buckle under newly added floor space. The city inspected 180 construction sites tied to companies working on the Pfizer building, including 24 conversions, and found no structural problems posing immediate public danger. Work has now restarted at the Pfizer site itself, where developer MetroLoft completed installation of new steel supports to replace damaged columns.

The accident set off scrutiny from lenders and developers reviewing their conversion projects, with investors examining sponsor experience more closely, according to BH3 Management principal Adam Falk. One new project will convert a 24-story downtown Brooklyn office tower completed in 2023 that never leased to tenants; BH3 and Capstone Equities bought the property at a discount and secured financing last month. The venture expects to complete the conversion in 18 to 20 months, compared with four to five years for ground-up construction. One-bedroom apartments in comparable Brooklyn buildings rent for about $5,000 monthly.

The city expects as many as 12,000 apartments from office conversions in coming years as part of its strategy to address housing shortages. Rising interest rates and construction costs have complicated project economics, while a recovering office market is giving some owners reason to reconsider conversions. Northwind Group founder Ran Eliasaf said the pace of new conversions will likely slow as developers exhaust the supply of buildings best suited for redevelopment, though his credit fund recently financed two conversions and has two more Midtown loans in the works.

item.title: New Fund Closes at $1.9 Billion as Office Hangover Sidelines Rivals
item.dc:creator: Propmodo Team
item.description:
Town Lane Management closes second fund at $1.9 billion, betting fresh capital and no legacy office exposure gives it edge over rivals.

The post New Fund Closes at $1.9 Billion as Office Hangover Sidelines Rivals appeared first on Propmodo.
item.content:encoded:
Town Lane Management closed its second real estate fund at $1.9 billion, exceeding its target by more than 25%. Founder Tyler Henritze, who spent nearly two decades at Blackstone before launching the firm with his sister Parker Morse in 2023, began marketing the vehicle in May. Commitments came from endowments, foundations, family offices and pension funds. Individual investments will range from $50 million to $300 million.

Henritze points to the firm’s lack of legacy holdings as a competitive advantage while older funds work through portfolios weighed down by office exposure and elevated interest rates. Commercial real estate values remain roughly 25% below their prior peak, according to JPMorgan Chase. Town Lane’s first fund, which raised $1.25 billion, backed senior housing, retail and small-business industrial properties. The firm also entered a joint venture with PowerHouse Data Centers to acquire land in North Carolina for a data center shell with power infrastructure.

Henritze left Blackstone in 2023, where he most recently served as head of strategic investments for real estate in the Americas and helped execute the acquisition of QTS Realty Trust. Town Lane has hired from TPG, Starwood Capital Group, Coatue Management and Blackstone. An advisory group includes former Blackstone executives Michael Nash and William Stein, and Guy Metcalfe, who led Morgan Stanley’s real estate investment banking business for more than two decades.

Ex-Blackstone Dealmaker Raises $1.9 Billion for Real Estate
